entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen2252" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Warning Against Self-Righteousness, Founded upon the Recital of Their Previous Sins - Deuteronomy 9-10:11</title> <div sID="gen2253" type="x-p"/> Besides the more vulgar pride which entirely forgets God, and attributes success and prosperity to its own power and exertion, there is one of a more refined character, which very easily spreads-namely, pride which acknowledges the blessings of God; but instead of receiving them gratefully, as unmerited gifts of the grace of the Lord, sees in them nothing but proofs of its own righteousness and virtue. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.9.4-Deut.9.6">Deu 9:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen2254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2255" type="x-p"/> When therefore Jehovah thrust out these nations before them (הדף, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.6.19">Deu 6:19</reference>), the Israelites were not to say within themselves, “<hi type="italic">By</hi> (for, on account of) <hi type="italic">my righteousness Jehovah hath brought me</hi> (led me hither) <hi type="italic">to possess this land</hi>.” The following word, וּברשׁעת, is adversative: “<hi type="italic">but because of the wickedness of these nations</hi>,” etc. - To impress this truth deeply upon the people, Moses repeats the thought once more in Deu 9:5. At the same time he mentions, in addition to righteousness, straightness or uprightness of heart, to indicate briefly that outward works do not constitute true righteousness, but that an upright state of heart is indispensable, and then enters more fully into the positive reasons. The wickedness of the Canaanites was no doubt a sufficient reason for destroying <hi type="italic">them</hi>, but not for giving their land to the people of Israel, since they could lay no claim to it on account of their own righteousness. The reason for giving Canaan to the Israelites was simply the promise of God, the word which the Lord had spoken to the patriarchs on oath (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.7.8">Deu 7:8</reference>), and therefore nothing but the free grace of God, - not any merit on the part of the Israelites who were then living, for they were a people “of a hard neck,” i.e., a stubborn, untractable generation. With these words, which the Lord Himself had applied to Israel in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.9">Exo 32:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.33.3">Exo 33:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.5">Exo 33:5</reference>, Moses prepares the way for passing to the reasons for his warning against self-righteous pride, namely, the grievous sins of the Israelites against the Lord.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.9.7-Deut.9.24">Deu 9:7-24</reference> <div eID="gen2255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2256" type="x-p"/> He reminded the people how they had provoked the Lord in the desert, and had shown themselves rebellious against God, from the day of their departure from Egypt till their arrival in the steppes of Moab. את־אשׁר, for אשׁר, is the object to תּשׁכּח (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §333, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.): “<hi type="italic">how</hi> thou hast provoked.” המרה, generally with את־פּי (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.1.26">Deu 1:26</reference>), to be rebellious against the commandment of the Lord: here with עם, construed with a person, to deal rebelliously <hi type="italic">with</hi> God, to act rebelliously in relation to Him (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.31.27">Deu 31:27</reference>). The words “<hi type="italic">from the day that thou camest out</hi>,” etc., are not to be pressed. It is to be observed, however, that the rebellion against the guidance of God commenced before they passed through the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.11">Exo 14:11</reference>). This general statement Moses then followed up with facts, first of all describing the worship of the calf at Horeb, according to its leading features (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.8-Deut.9.21">Deu 9:8-21</reference>), and then briefly pointing to the other rebellions of the people in the desert (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.22">Deu 9:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.23">Deu 9:23</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.9.25-Deut.9.29">Deu 9:25-29</reference> <div eID="gen2260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2261" type="x-p"/> After vindicating in this way the thought expressed in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.7">Deu 9:7</reference>, by enumerating the principal rebellions of the people against their God, Moses returns in Deu 9:25. to the apostasy at Sinai, for the purpose of showing still further how Israel had no righteousness or ground for boasting before God, and owed its preservation, with all the saving blessings of the covenant, solely to the mercy of God and His covenant faithfulness. To this end he repeats in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.26-Deut.9.29">Deu 9:26-29</reference> the essential points in his intercession for the people after their sin at Sinai, and then proceeds to explain still further, in <reference osisRef="Deut.10.1-Deut.10.11">Deu 10:1-11</reference>, how the Lord had not only renewed the tables of the covenant in consequence of this intercession (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.1-Deut.10.5">Deu 10:1-5</reference>), but had also established the gracious institution of the priesthood for the time to come by appointing Eleazar in Aaron’s stead as soon as his father died, and setting apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant and attend to the holy service, and had commanded them to continue their march to Canaan, and take possession of the land promised to the fathers (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.6-Deut.10.11">Deu 10:6-11</reference>). With the words “thus I fell down,” in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.25">Deu 9:25</reference>, Moses returns to the intercession already briefly mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.18">Deu 9:18</reference>, and recalls to the recollection of the people the essential features of his plea at the time. For the words “<hi type="italic">the forty days and nights that I fell down</hi>,” see at Deu 1:46. The substance of the intercession in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.26-Deut.9.29">Deu 9:26-29</reference> is essentially the same as that in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.11-Exod.32.13">Exo 32:11-13</reference>; but given with such freedom as any other than Moses would hardly have allowed himself (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>), and in such a manner as to bring it into the most obvious relation to the words of God in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.12">Deu 9:12</reference>, Deu 9:13. אל־תּשׁחת, “<hi type="italic">Destroy not Thy people and Thine inheritance</hi>,” says Moses, with reference to the words of the Lord to him: “<hi type="italic">thy people have corrupted themselves</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.12">Deu 9:12</reference>). Israel was not Moses’ nation, but the nation and inheritance of Jehovah; it was not Moses, but Jehovah, who had brought it out of Egypt. True, the people were stiffnecked (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.9.13">Deu 9:13</reference>); but let the Lord remember the fathers, the oath given to Abraham, which is expressly mentioned in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.13">Exo 32:13</reference> (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.7.8">Deu 7:8</reference>), and not turn to the stiffneckedness of the people (קשׁי equivalent to ערף קשׁה, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.13">Deu 9:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.9.6">Deu 9:6</reference>), and to their wickedness and sin (i.e., not regard them and punish them). The honour of the Lord before the nations was concerned in this (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.28">Deu 9:28</reference>). The land whence Israel came out (“the land” = the people of the land, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.10.25">Gen 10:25</reference>, etc., viz., the Egyptians: the word is construed as a collective with a plural verb) must not have occasion to say, that Jehovah had not led His people into the promised land from incapacity or hatred. יכלת מבּלי recalls Num 14:16. Just as “inability” would be opposed to the nature of the absolute God, so “hatred” would be opposed to the choice of Israel as the inheritance of Jehovah, which He had brought out of Egypt by His divine and almighty power (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.6.6">Exo 6:6</reference>).  <chapter eID="Deut.9"/> <div eID="gen2261" type="x-p"/>

The substance of the intercession in Deu 9:26-29 is essentially the same as that in Exo 32:11-13; but given with such freedom as any other than Moses would hardly have allowed himself (Schultz), and in such a manner as to bring it into the most obvious relation to the words of God in Deu 9:12, Deu 9:13. אל־תּשׁחת, “Destroy not Thy people and Thine inheritance,” says Moses, with reference to the words of the Lord to him: “thy people have corrupted themselves” (Deu 9:12). Israel was not Moses’ nation, but the nation and inheritance of Jehovah; it was not Moses, but Jehovah, who had brought it out of Egypt. True, the people were stiffnecked (cf. Deu 9:13); but let the Lord remember the fathers, the oath given to Abraham, which is expressly mentioned in Exo 32:13 (see at Deu 7:8), and not turn to the stiffneckedness of the people (קשׁי equivalent to ערף קשׁה, Deu 9:13 and Deu 9:6), and to their wickedness and sin (i.e., not regard them and punish them). The honour of the Lord before the nations was concerned in this (Deu 9:28). The land whence Israel came out (“the land” = the people of the land, as in Gen 10:25, etc., viz., the Egyptians: the word is construed as a collective with a plural verb) must not have occasion to say, that Jehovah had not led His people into the promised land from incapacity or hatred. יכלת מבּלי recalls Num 14:16. Just as “inability” would be opposed to the nature of the absolute God, so “hatred” would be opposed to the choice of Israel as the inheritance of Jehovah, which He had brought out of Egypt by His divine and almighty power (cf. Exo 6:6).
